title: Payment system
prompt: Design the payment backend for a marketplace: buyers pay by card through an external processor, sellers are paid out weekly, and finance needs an accurate ledger.

requirements: Functional: charge a buyer, record fees, refund, pay out sellers, and show balances.
Correctness first: never charge twice, never lose money, every movement is traceable; latency matters less than accuracy.
Clarify: currencies, compliance (avoid storing raw card numbers: use the processor’s tokens).
estimation: 1M payments a day ≈ 12/s average; peaks of a few hundred per second on sale days. Volume is modest; correctness is the challenge.
Each payment creates several ledger entries (buyer, seller, fees), so a few million rows a day, kept for years.
api: POST /payments {orderId, amount, currency, paymentMethodToken} with an Idempotency-Key → {paymentId, status}.
Processor webhooks: POST /webhooks/processor, signed and deduplicated by event ID.
data: Amounts as integers in minor units (cents) plus currency; never floating point.
payments(id, order_id, idempotency_key UNIQUE, amount, status, processor_ref, version) as a state machine.
ledger_entries(id, transaction_id, account_id, amount, direction) append-only; each transaction’s debits equal its credits (double-entry).
outbox(id, event, created_at) written in the same transaction as state changes.
design: Payment service records a pending payment, then calls the processor with the same idempotency key.
On success it updates status and writes balanced ledger entries in one transaction; an outbox relay publishes events (receipt, order paid).
Webhooks confirm final states; a nightly reconciliation compares internal records with processor settlement reports.
Payout jobs read seller balances from the ledger and initiate bank transfers, also idempotently.
deepDives: Unknown outcomes: if the processor call times out, do not blindly retry with a new key; query by idempotency key or wait for the webhook, then resolve.
Double-entry: every transaction sums to zero across accounts, so errors show up as imbalances; corrections are new reversing entries, never edits.
Transactional outbox: avoids the “database committed but event lost” failure that a separate publish call would have.
bottlenecks: Hot accounts (the platform fee account) see every transaction: shard with sub-accounts and sum them, or compute balances asynchronously.
Processor outages: queue and retry with the same keys, show “processing” to buyers, fail over to a second processor where contracts allow.
Audit and access: restrict who can write ledger data; log every change.
tradeoffs: Strong consistency and immutable ledgers cost throughput, but money demands them.
Synchronous charge gives instant answers; asynchronous with webhooks is more robust to timeouts. Most systems combine them.
A second processor improves availability but doubles integration and reconciliation work.

rubric.text: Used idempotency keys end to end, including with the processor.
Stored money as integer minor units with currency.
Modelled payment state transitions and handled unknown outcomes.
Published events reliably (transactional outbox or equivalent).
Reconciled internal records against the processor.
Handled hot accounts and processor failover.
Covered compliance: tokenisation, audit trails and access control.
